lead: A continuous prestressed beam is statically indeterminate. Prestress can then produce reactions at supports even when no external load acts. These secondary reactions shift the pressure line and complicate design. A concordant cable is a tendon profile that produces no such reactions: the pressure line coincides with the cable. Linear transformation is the rule that lets you move a cable profile by adding a straight line without changing the equivalent loads. Designers use it to adjust tendon eccentricity for cover, anchorage or stress while keeping the load balancing and reactions unchanged.
prereq: You need: load balancing and equivalent loads from 6.4, and continuous beam bending from Unit 2.

blocks.text: A simply supported prestressed beam is statically determinate. The beam can bend freely under prestress, so the supports feel no vertical force from the tendon. Every cable in such a beam is concordant.

A continuous beam is statically indeterminate. The middle support restrains the beam, so prestress can create reactions at the supports. These reactions are called secondary reactions. They produce a secondary bending moment Ms in addition to the primary moment P e.

The pressure line is the locus of the resultant compressive force in the concrete. Its eccentricity from the centroid is ep = M / P, where M is the total moment from prestress (primary plus secondary), P is the prestress force, and ep is measured from the centroid, positive downward. In a concordant cable, ep(x) = e(x) at every section, so Ms = 0 and the support reactions from prestress are zero.

A straight cable at constant eccentricity is the simplest concordant cable in a two-span beam. It gives a constant moment P e and zero shear, so the supports feel no vertical force. A concentric straight cable with e = 0 is a trivial case. A curved cable can also be concordant if its equivalent loads are self-equilibrated. The test is zero secondary reactions, not zero eccentricity.

Concordant profiles are useful because the designer can analyse prestress alone without computing secondary moments. They also avoid unexpected reactions at supports. In practice many tendons are not concordant, so secondary reactions must be calculated.

A linear transformation of a cable profile means adding a straight line: enew(x) = e(x) + a + b x. Here x is the distance along the beam (m), a is a constant with units of length (m), and b is dimensionless — it is the slope of the added line, in m/m. The added term has zero curvature, d²(a + b x)/dx² = 0.

blocks.where: w_p is the equivalent upward load per unit length (N/m); P is the prestress force (N); e is the tendon eccentricity, positive downward (m); x is the distance along the beam (m).

blocks.text: A sagging parabola has negative second derivative, so wp is positive, i.e. upward. Because the added straight line has zero second derivative, it does not change wp.

In a continuous beam, the reactions from prestress come from the complete equivalent load system: the distributed loads wp, the anchorage forces and moments at the ends, and the support conditions. A linear transformation does change the anchorage forces and moments, but that change is self-equilibrated: zero net force and zero net moment. A self-equilibrated change adds no support reaction. So the reactions depend only on wp and the support conditions, and wp is unchanged. Therefore a linear transformation of a concordant cable is also concordant. This is the theorem of linear transformation.

What changes is the eccentricity and the primary moment P e at every section. Stresses and cover change. Linear transformation is not free for stress design; it only preserves the equivalent loads and the reactions. Designers use it to shift a tendon up or down at a support, to satisfy anchorage or cover, without changing the load balancing.

Take a two-span beam with equal spans L. A straight tendon at constant eccentricity e = 100 mm is concordant. The moment is P × 0.100 at every section, the shear is zero, and the middle support feels no vertical force from prestress.

Add a straight line et = k x/L, with k in mm and x measured from the left end. The beam is 2L long, so at the right end x = 2L. The new profile is a straight inclined tendon: at the left end e = 100 mm, at the right end e = 100 + 2k mm. The curvature is still zero, so wp = 0 and the reactions are still zero. The moment becomes linear. The cable remains concordant.

A parabolic tendon in each span is different. Its curvature is not zero, so it produces an equivalent load wp. That load generally needs support reactions, so the cable is not concordant unless the equivalent loads are self-equilibrated. Linear transformation still leaves wp unchanged, so it cannot turn a non-concordant cable into a concordant one. It only preserves whatever reactions already exist.

In post-tensioned continuous slabs and beams, designers often choose a concordant profile or accept secondary moments. The equivalent load method from 6.4 gives wp; the linear transformation rule then lets the tendon be moved for practical detailing without recomputing that load.

figure.caption: A straight line added to the tendon profile changes e(x) but not its curvature. The equivalent load w_p and, for a concordant cable, the support reactions stay the same.

spec.title: Linear transformation
spec.aria: Adding a straight line to a cable profile changes eccentricity but not curvature, so the equivalent upward load and the reactions stay the same.

examples.question: A simply supported prestressed concrete beam has span L = 12 m. A parabolic tendon has zero eccentricity at both ends and midspan eccentricity e = 120 mm below the centroid. The prestress force is P = 800 kN. (a) Find the equivalent upward load w_p. (b) A straight line e_t = 40x/L mm is added to the profile, with x in metres. Find the eccentricity at midspan and the new equivalent load.
steps: Write the parabolic profile: e(x) = 4 e_mid x(L − x)/L². Its second derivative is −8 e_mid/L².
Convert units: P = 800 kN = 800,000 N; e = 120 mm = 0.120 m; L = 12 m.
For the added line, e_t = 40x/12 = 3.333x mm. At midspan x = 6 m, e_t = 40 × 6 / 12 = 20 mm.
The second derivative of e_t is zero, so it adds no equivalent load. The new w_p is still 5333.33 N/m = 5.33 kN/m upward.
examples.answer: The equivalent upward load is 5333.33 N/m (5.33 kN/m); adding the straight line gives a midspan eccentricity of 140 mm and leaves the equivalent load unchanged at 5333.33 N/m.
examples.check:

wp = 8*P*e/L**2
print(f"{wp:.2f}")
et_mid = 40.0*6.0/12.0
print(f"{et_mid:.2f}")
e_new = 120.0 + et_mid
print(f"{e_new:.2f}")
print(f"{wp:.2f}")

traps: Concordant does not mean straight or concentric. Concordant means zero secondary reactions; a curved cable can be concordant if its equivalent loads are self-equilibrated, and a straight concentric cable is only a trivial case.
Adding a straight line does not change w_p. Do not recompute w_p from the new midspan eccentricity; use the curvature, which comes only from the parabolic part.
Secondary reactions are not external loads. They are caused by restraint in a continuous beam. A simply supported beam has none.
Watch the sign in w_p = −P d²e/dx². With e positive downward, a sagging parabola has e'' negative and gives upward w_p.
The pressure line equals the cable only when the cable is concordant. In general e_p = M/P includes the secondary moment, so the pressure line is not the tendon profile.

quiz.a: A cable whose pressure line coincides with the cable itself, so prestress produces zero support reactions.

quiz.q: State the linear transformation rule for tendon profiles.
quiz.a: Adding a straight line a + bx to the eccentricity profile leaves the curvature and hence the equivalent load w_p unchanged; if the original cable was concordant, the new one is also concordant.

quiz.q: Why does a simply supported beam have no secondary reactions from prestress?
quiz.a: It is statically determinate. The beam can bend freely, so the tendon force does not create support reactions. Every cable is concordant.

quiz.q: A two-span beam has a straight tendon at constant e = 100 mm. Is it concordant? Explain.
quiz.a: Yes. The moment is constant P × 0.100, the shear is zero, and the supports feel no vertical force from prestress.

quiz.q: A parabolic tendon has L = 10 m, e_mid = 100 mm, P = 600 kN. Find w_p.
In the worked example, if a straight line of 30 mm at midspan is added, find the new midspan eccentricity and w_p.
quiz.a: e_new = 120 + 30 = 150 mm. w_p is unchanged at 5333.33 N/m because the added line has zero curvature.

quiz.q: A non-concordant cable has nonzero w_p. Does a linear transformation make it concordant? Explain.
quiz.a: No. Linear transformation leaves w_p and the reactions unchanged. It only preserves concordance if the original reactions were zero.

quiz.q: Why can linear transformation adjust tendon cover without changing load balancing?
quiz.a: It changes e and the primary moment P e, so stresses and cover change. But it adds zero curvature, so w_p = −P e'' and the balanced load are unchanged.

beyond: Not for the exam. In practice, continuous post-tensioned slabs and bridge decks often have secondary moments. Software computes them by equivalent loads or finite elements. Concordant profiles are used to avoid unexpected reactions in transfer beams. Search for 'secondary moments prestressed continuous beam', 'linear transformation theorem tendon', and 'concordant cable pressure line'.
